about: Sourced life stories for the Persian kings Scripture names from the fall of Babylon to Nehemiah, the queens Vashti and Esther, and the governors Gedaliah, Zerubbabel and Nehemiah. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/rulers-persia.md.

darius-dan-5-31.short: Darius the Mede took the kingdom of the Chaldeans when Belshazzar was slain, made Daniel first of his presidents, and decreed that men should fear the God of Daniel.

paragraphs.text: Scripture knows Darius the Mede only from the book of Daniel and says little about his own life. Daniel calls him “Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans”. On the night that Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans was slain, “Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old”.

He set a hundred and twenty princes over the kingdom and three presidents over them, of whom Daniel was first, and he thought to set Daniel over the whole realm. The presidents and princes could find no fault in Daniel, so they asked the king to sign a decree that for thirty days anyone who asked a petition of any god or man except the king should be cast into the den of lions; “king Darius signed the writing and the decree”.

When Daniel was found praying to his God, his accusers told the king of it and of the decree. Darius was “sore displeased with himself” and laboured until sunset to deliver him, but they reminded him that by “the law of the Medes and Persians” no decree the king made might be changed, and Daniel was cast into the den. The king sealed the stone with his own signet, passed the night fasting, and went in haste to the den very early in the morning, where Daniel answered him unhurt. Then he had Daniel's accusers cast into the den with their children and their wives.

Darius wrote to “all people, nations, and languages” that in every dominion of his kingdom men should “tremble and fear before the God of Daniel: for he is the living God”. Daniel prospered in his reign and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian. Daniel dates to Darius's first year the time when he understood from Jeremiah's words the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolations, and in Daniel 11 the one speaking to Daniel says that in that first year he stood “to confirm and to strengthen him”; Michael has just been named, and the verse does not say plainly whom “him” means. Scripture does not say how long Darius reigned or how he died.

cyrus-2ch-36-22.short: Cyrus king of Persia, whom Isaiah calls the LORD's shepherd, proclaimed in his first year that the LORD's people might go up and build his house at Jerusalem.

paragraphs.text: Scripture calls him “Cyrus king of Persia” and “Cyrus the Persian”, and says nothing of his family. Isaiah names him as the one of whom the LORD says, “He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure”, and calls him the LORD's “anointed”, whose right hand the LORD had held “to subdue nations before him”. The LORD says to him, “I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me”, and says that he would build the LORD's city and “let go my captives, not for price nor reward”.

Chronicles and Ezra say that in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia “the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus”, that the word spoken by Jeremiah might be fulfilled. He made a proclamation throughout his kingdom and put it in writing: the LORD God of heaven had given him all the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build him a house at Jerusalem, and any of the LORD's people might go up and build it, helped by their neighbours with silver, gold, goods and beasts. Chronicles ends its record of the proclamation at “let him go up”.

Cyrus brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried from Jerusalem and put in the house of his gods, and by Mithredath the treasurer numbered them to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah: five thousand four hundred vessels of gold and silver. The children of the captivity came up to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel and others, and gave meat, drink and oil to the men of Zidon and Tyre to bring cedar from Lebanon “according to the grant that they had of Cyrus king of Persia”.

When the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin asked to build with them, Zerubbabel and Jeshua refused, saying they would build “as king Cyrus the king of Persia hath commanded us”. The people of the land troubled the builders “all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia”. In the reign of Darius a roll was found at Achmetha recording that in his first year Cyrus had ordered the house built, its costs paid from the king's house, and the vessels restored.

Daniel prospered in the reign of Cyrus the Persian; he continued to the first year of king Cyrus, and dated a vision to “the third year of Cyrus king of Persia”. Scripture does not tell how long Cyrus reigned or how he died.

zerubbabel-1ch-3-19.short: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel led the exiles who came up from Babylon, led the rebuilding of the LORD's house, and was governor of Judah.

paragraphs.text: Ezra, Nehemiah and Haggai call him “Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel”, and Matthew writes “Salathiel begat Zorobabel”. First Chronicles instead lists him among the sons of Pedaiah, who is named among the sons of Jeconiah, and names among Zerubbabel's own children Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith. Matthew names his son as Abiud.

He came up out of the captivity at the head of the list of those who returned to Jerusalem and Judah. In the seventh month Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brethren the priests, with Zerubbabel and his brethren, built the altar of the God of Israel, offered burnt offerings morning and evening, and kept the feast of tabernacles. Ezra also tells of Sheshbazzar, “the prince of Judah”, to whom Cyrus numbered the temple vessels; Scripture does not say whether he and Zerubbabel are one man, and the question is taken up on his page as a ruler.

In the second month of the second year after their coming, Zerubbabel and Jeshua set the Levites over the work of the house of the LORD. When the foundation was laid the people shouted with a great shout, while many of the old men who had seen the first house wept with a loud voice. When the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin asked to build with them, Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the chief of the fathers answered, “Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God”. The people of the land troubled the builders, and the work stopped until the second year of Darius king of Persia.

In the second year of Darius the word of the LORD came by Haggai “unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah”, and to Joshua the high priest, because the LORD's house lay waste. The LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, of Joshua and of the remnant of the people, and on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month they came and worked on the house. In the seventh month Haggai told him, “Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the LORD”.

On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month Haggai brought a word addressed to Zerubbabel: the LORD would shake the heavens and the earth, and “will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee”. Zechariah records a word of the LORD to him, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts”, and a word that the hands of Zerubbabel, which had laid the foundation of the house, would also finish it.

Ezra says the house was finished on the third day of Adar in the sixth year of Darius, with the elders of the Jews building and prospering through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah; Zerubbabel is not named at its finishing. Nehemiah records that “all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel” gave the portions of the singers and the porters. Scripture does not say when his time as governor ended or how he died.

darius-ezr-4-5.short: Darius king of Persia, in whose second year the building of the LORD's house began again, confirmed Cyrus's decree and paid for the work and the sacrifices.

paragraphs.text: Scripture tells little of Darius himself: it does not say how he came to the throne, how long he reigned or how he died. Ezra calls him “Darius king of Persia” and names him after Cyrus: the people of the land troubled the builders “all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia”, and the work on the house ceased “unto the second year of the reign of Darius”.

In his second year the prophets Haggai and Zechariah dated their words by his reign, and Zerubbabel, Joshua and the remnant of the people began again to build. Tatnai, governor on this side the river, asked who had commanded the work, and wrote to Darius asking that the records at Babylon be searched for the decree of Cyrus.

Darius made a decree and the search was made; at Achmetha, in the province of the Medes, a roll was found recording Cyrus's command to build the house. Darius told Tatnai to let the work alone, to pay its costs from the tribute beyond the river, and to supply what the priests at Jerusalem appointed for the burnt offerings “day by day without fail”, that they might “pray for the life of the king, and of his sons”. He decreed that anyone who altered his word should be hanged on timber pulled down from his own house, and ended, “I Darius have made a decree; let it be done with speed”.

Tatnai and his companions did speedily as Darius had sent. In his fourth year the word of the LORD came to Zechariah about the fasts of the fifth and seventh months. The house was finished on the third day of the month Adar “in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king” and dedicated with joy; at the Passover that followed, Ezra says, the LORD had turned the heart of “the king of Assyria” to the people, to strengthen their hands in the work of the house of God.

ahasuerus-ezr-4-6.short: Ahasuerus reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces; he removed Queen Vashti, made Esther queen, and gave his ring to Haman against the Jews, then to Mordecai.

paragraphs.text: Scripture tells of King Ahasuerus in the book of Esther, and names an Ahasuerus once in Ezra, where in the beginning of his reign the enemies of Judah wrote him an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem; it does not say whether these are the same king. It names no parents or children for him. Esther says he “reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces”, and sat on his throne in Shushan the palace.

In his third year he made a feast for his princes and servants that lasted a hundred and eighty days, and then a seven-day feast for all the people in Shushan. On the seventh day, when his heart was “merry with wine”, he sent for Queen Vashti to show her beauty; she refused, and on the counsel of Memucan he decreed that she “come no more before king Ahasuerus”.

When his wrath was appeased he “remembered Vashti”, and young women were gathered to Shushan so that the one who pleased him might be queen. In the tenth month of his seventh year Esther was taken to him; he loved her above all the women, set the royal crown on her head, and made a great feast. Through Esther, Mordecai warned him of a plot by two of his chamberlains, and it was written in the book of the chronicles.

He promoted Haman the Agagite above all his princes, and in his twelfth year gave Haman his ring to seal letters ordering that all the Jews in his provinces be destroyed on the thirteenth day of Adar. On a night when he could not sleep he had the chronicles read, learned that nothing had been done for Mordecai, and had Haman lead Mordecai through the city on horseback in royal apparel. At Esther's second banquet, when she named Haman as the enemy of her people, he had Haman hanged on the gallows Haman had made for Mordecai.

He gave his ring to Mordecai and let Esther and Mordecai write for the Jews in his name, for a writing sealed with the king's ring “may no man reverse”; the new letters allowed the Jews to stand for their lives. He laid a tribute on the land and on the isles of the sea, and his acts are written “in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia”. Scripture does not say how long he reigned or how he died.

vashti-est-1-9.short: Vashti was queen beside King Ahasuerus; she refused to come at his command, and he decreed that she come no more before him.

paragraphs.text: Scripture knows Vashti only from the opening of the book of Esther, and names no family or children for her. Esther calls her “Vashti the queen” and “the queen Vashti”. While King Ahasuerus feasted the people of Shushan, she “made a feast for the women in the royal house which belonged to king Ahasuerus”.

On the seventh day of the feast, when the king's heart was “merry with wine”, he sent seven chamberlains to bring Vashti before him with the crown royal, to show the people and the princes her beauty, “for she was fair to look on”. She refused to come, and the king was very angry. Scripture does not say why she refused.

The king asked his wise men what should be done to her by law. Memucan answered that her deed would lead all women to despise their husbands, and advised a royal decree, written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that she “come no more before king Ahasuerus” and that her “royal estate” be given to another; the king did so and sent letters to every province. Her place as queen was the king's to give, and Esther was later made queen “instead of Vashti”.
When his wrath was appeased the king “remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her”. Scripture says nothing more of her or of what became of her.

esther-est-2-7.short: Esther, also called Hadassah, an orphan brought up by her cousin Mordecai, became queen beside King Ahasuerus and pleaded with him for the lives of her people.

paragraphs.text: Esther, whose other name was Hadassah, was the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai. Mordecai was a Jew in Shushan the palace, “the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite”. Her father and mother were dead, and Mordecai brought her up and took her “for his own daughter”. The text says “the maid was fair and beautiful”.

When the king sought a new queen in place of Vashti, Esther was taken with many young women into the king's house, into the keeping of Hegai, keeper of the women. She pleased Hegai and obtained kindness of him, and at Mordecai's charge she did not make known her people or her kindred, while Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women's house to know how she did. When her turn came to go in to the king she asked for nothing but what Hegai appointed, and she “obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her”.

She was taken to King Ahasuerus in the tenth month, Tebeth, of his seventh year. The king loved her above all the women, “set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti”, and made a great feast, Esther's feast. She was queen beside the king; Scripture does not say that she reigned. She still did as Mordecai told her, and when he learned of a plot by two chamberlains against the king, she told the king of it in Mordecai's name.

In the king's twelfth year Haman obtained a decree, sealed with the king's ring, that all the Jews be destroyed on one day. When Mordecai charged Esther to go to the king for her people, she answered that anyone who came to the king in the inner court uncalled was put to death unless the king held out the golden sceptre, and she had not been called for thirty days. Mordecai sent back, “who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” Esther asked the Jews in Shushan to fast for her three days, she and her maidens with them, and said, “so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.”

On the third day she put on her royal apparel and stood in the inner court; the king held out the golden sceptre, and she touched its top. She invited the king and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second. There she asked, “let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request”, and named “this wicked Haman” as the enemy; the king had Haman hanged on the gallows he had made for Mordecai, and gave Esther the house of Haman.

Esther told the king what Mordecai was to her and set him over the house of Haman; then she fell at the king's feet and with tears asked that Haman's letters be reversed: “how can I endure to see the evil that shall come unto my people?” The king let her and Mordecai write for the Jews in his name, and at her further request the Jews in Shushan were given a second day and Haman's ten sons were hanged. Then “Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority” to confirm the days of Purim, and “the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book.” Scripture does not say how long she was queen, whether she had children, or when she died.

artaxerxes-ezr-4-7.short: Under the name Artaxerxes, Ezra and Nehemiah tell of a halt to Jerusalem's building, Ezra sent with the king's gifts, and Nehemiah sent to rebuild the wall.

paragraphs.text: Scripture tells nothing of Artaxerxes' family or life beyond his dealings with Jerusalem; it mentions his sons, and a queen who sat by him, but names neither. Ezra 4 names him after Ahasuerus, Ezra 7 sets Ezra's journey “in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia”, and Nehemiah was cupbearer to “Artaxerxes the king”. Scripture does not say whether one king is meant in all these places.

Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote to him that the Jews were building “the rebellious and the bad city” and setting up its walls, and that if it were built the king would lose his tribute beyond the river. Artaxerxes had the records searched, found that the city had rebelled against kings of old, and ordered that the men be made to cease “until another commandment shall be given from me”. Rehum, Shimshai and their companions went up to Jerusalem in haste and “made them to cease by force and power”.

In his seventh year he gave Ezra the priest, a scribe of the law, a letter beginning “Artaxerxes, king of kings, unto Ezra the priest”. It let any of Israel who wished go up with Ezra, sent silver and gold that the king and his counsellors had offered to the God of Israel, ordered his treasurers beyond the river to supply Ezra, freed the priests and Levites from toll and tribute, and charged Ezra to set magistrates and judges over the people beyond the river and to teach the laws of his God to those who did not know them; “for why should there be wrath against the realm of the king and his sons?” Ezra blessed the LORD, who had “put such a thing as this in the king's heart”.

In the month Nisan of his twentieth year his cupbearer Nehemiah came before him with a sad face. When Nehemiah asked to be sent to build the city of his fathers' sepulchres, the king, with the queen sitting by him, asked how long he would be gone, gave him letters to the governors beyond the river and for timber from the king's forest, and sent captains and horsemen with him. Nehemiah was governor of Judah from that twentieth year to the king's thirty-second, when he came back to the king and after certain days obtained leave again. Scripture does not say how long Artaxerxes reigned or how he died.

nehemiah-neh-1-1.short: Nehemiah son of Hachaliah, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, went to Jerusalem as governor of Judah and rebuilt its wall in fifty-two days.

paragraphs.text: Nehemiah was the son of Hachaliah, and Hanani was his brother. In the month Chisleu of the twentieth year, in Shushan the palace, Hanani and men of Judah told him that the remnant in the province were in great affliction and that the wall of Jerusalem was broken down and its gates burned. He sat down and wept, mourned certain days, fasted and prayed, confessing that “both I and my father's house have sinned”, and asked God for mercy “in the sight of this man”: he was the king's cupbearer.

In Nisan of the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, the king saw that his face was sad, and Nehemiah, “very sore afraid”, told him that the city of his fathers' sepulchres lay waste. He prayed to the God of heaven and asked to be sent to Judah to build it; the king, the queen sitting by him, granted it, with letters to the governors beyond the river and for timber from the king's forest, “according to the good hand of my God upon me”. He came with captains and horsemen, and Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite were grieved that a man had come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.

Three days after he came to Jerusalem he went out by night with a few men and viewed the broken walls and burned gates, telling no one what God had put in his heart. Then he said to the Jews and their rulers, “let us build up the wall of Jerusalem”, and they answered, “Let us rise up and build.” Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem the Arabian mocked them, and when Sanballat and Tobiah conspired with others to fight against Jerusalem, he prayed, set a watch, and armed the people by families; the builders worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other.

When the people cried out that they had mortgaged their lands and were bringing their sons and daughters into bondage, Nehemiah was “very angry”, rebuked the nobles and rulers for exacting usury, and took an oath of them that they would restore what they had taken. In his twelve years as governor, from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, he did not burden the people as the former governors had, “because of the fear of God”, and did not eat “the bread of the governor”, though a hundred and fifty Jews and rulers ate at his table. He prayed, “Think upon me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people.”

His enemies asked him four times to meet them in the plain of Ono, and the fifth time sent an open letter saying he meant to be king; he answered, “There are no such things done as thou sayest.” When Shemaiah urged him to hide in the temple, he said, “Should such a man as I flee?”, and perceived that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. The wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, “in fifty and two days”. When Ezra read the law, Nehemiah, “which is the Tirshatha”, with Ezra and the Levites told the weeping people, “This day is holy unto the LORD your God; mourn not, nor weep.” His name stands first among those who sealed the covenant, and at the dedication of the wall he went with one of the two companies that gave thanks.

In the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes he went back to the king, and after certain days returned to Jerusalem. He threw Tobiah's household stuff out of the chamber that Eliashib the priest had prepared for him in the courts of the house of God, gathered back the Levites whose portions had not been given, shut the gates of Jerusalem against the sabbath traders, and contended with Jews who had married wives of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab. His book ends with his prayer, “Remember me, O my God, for good.” Scripture does not say when or where he died.

gedaliah-2ki-25-22.short: Gedaliah son of Ahikam was made governor over the people left in Judah after Jerusalem fell, and was murdered at Mizpah by Ishmael son of Nethaniah.

paragraphs.text: Gedaliah was the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan; the book of Jeremiah says that “the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah”, so that the prophet was not given to the people to be put to death. After Nebuchadnezzar's captain of the guard came to Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king's nineteenth year and burned it, the king of Babylon made Gedaliah ruler over the people left in the land of Judah: men, women and children, and of the poor of the land.

The princes of Babylon took Jeremiah out of the court of the prison and committed him to Gedaliah, and Nebuzar-adan the captain of the guard let Jeremiah go back to him; Jeremiah went to Gedaliah at Mizpah and dwelt with him among the people left in the land. The captains of the forces came to him there, Ishmael son of Nethaniah and Johanan son of Kareah among them, and he swore to them, “Fear not to serve the Chaldeans: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you.” Jews who had been driven into Moab, Ammon, Edom and other lands came back to him and gathered wine and summer fruits “very much”.

Johanan and the captains warned him that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael to kill him, and Johanan offered to kill Ishmael secretly, lest the remnant in Judah perish. “But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam believed them not”, and told Johanan, “thou speakest falsely of Ishmael.”

In the seventh month Ishmael, “of the seed royal”, came to Mizpah with ten men, and they ate bread together; then Ishmael and his men struck Gedaliah with the sword and killed him, with the Jews and the Chaldeans who were with him. Scripture does not say in which year this happened. Afterwards the people and the captains, afraid of the Chaldeans, went to Egypt, taking with them everyone whom Nebuzar-adan had left with Gedaliah, and Jeremiah too.
